cards.name: Supporters and atmosphere
cards.a: About 218,000 members (2025). Every home match full (about 81,000), the highest average crowd in world football. About 5,400 travel to away matches. Fans' pyrotechnics cost €139,000 in fines by February 2026; the standing terrace was closed for one match in 2017 after attacks on visiting fans.
cards.b: About 72,000 members. Every home match full (about 22,000), mostly standing. About 3,100 travel to away matches. Fans' pyrotechnics cost €242,000 in fines by February 2026, then a club-record €340,000 for one anniversary display; a fan's thrown lighter cost the team a 2024 draw.

cards.name: The ground
cards.a: Opened 1974, about 3 km from the city centre; World Cup venue in 1974 and 2006. 81,365 places, including a single standing terrace of about 25,000. Sold in a 2002 cash crisis, bought back in 2006, club-owned since. Named after a local insurer until 2031. No move planned.
cards.b: Opened 1920 in a wooded suburb; over 2,300 fans rebuilt the terraces as volunteers in 2008. 22,012 places, about 18,000 standing. Owned by a club company whose shares fans bought. A €190m expansion to 35,000-40,000 means 18 months at the city's Olympic stadium from 2028.

cards.name: Ownership and governance
cards.a: A company listed on the stock exchange since 2000. The members' association owns about 5% of the shares but all of the managing company, so members keep control. Members elect the president directly: the former chief executive, elected unopposed in 2025 with 59%. Lost €22m last season.
cards.b: A members' association; the professional team was never moved into a company. Members elect a supervisory board, which appoints the president: the same man since 2004, now full-time until 2029. In 2011 it emerged he did 1980s national service in a secret-police guard regiment. Breaking even.

cards.name: Fans' say in the club
cards.a: Members vote at the annual meeting and elect the president. In 2024 they voted 556-247 to end an arms-maker sponsorship; the vote was not binding and the deal runs to its 2027 end. The outgoing president, who had turned against the deal, withdrew from re-election in 2025.
cards.b: Members vote at the annual meeting and elect the supervisory board (the chairman's list of six was re-elected in 2026). The president is appointed by that board, not elected. The fan-and-members department holds a board seat; fan clubs fielded their own candidate for the first time in 2026.

cards.name: Community work and causes
cards.a: Stadium rules against racism and the far right since 2007, proposed by fans. Turned a planned fan house into winter refugee housing in 2015; a club-linked charity helps refugees find work and homes; a food bank runs at the ground. Lifetime ban for antisemitic abuse (2021). No Pride activity found.
cards.b: A club foundation since 2012 with 100-plus projects. Holocaust-education trips for fans since 2008, a €1m gift to a Holocaust memorial, an anti-discrimination officer. A gay and lesbian fan club is part of the terrace. Integration projects for young refugees. Far-right hooligan groups in the 1980s.

cards.name: Sponsors
cards.a: Shirt: a telecoms group (to 2030), also on the women's shirts. Stadium: a local insurer. Top-tier partners include an arms maker (to 2027, opposed by members) and a betting firm (to 2028, also backing the women's team). Several shareholders are sponsors: a chemicals group, the insurer, the kit maker.
cards.b: Shirt: a local savings-platform fintech (since 2025), also on the women's shirts. Sleeve: a heat-pump maker. A betting firm was a top sponsor 2018-2024; current betting ties not confirmed. No arms or state-owned partner found. About 300 partners in all.

cards.name: The women's team
cards.a: Founded 1969. Professional since 2023; promoted twice in two seasons to the top flight (2025) and finished 9th of 14 there. Plays at the men's ground; record crowd 14,047. Coached by a woman who in 2026 became the league's first female head coach of a men's top-flight team.
cards.b: Founded 2021, starting in the seventh tier; four straight promotions, now third tier and top after six matches. Plays at a 10,000-capacity ground beside the main stadium; record crowd 15,755 (2025 cup tie against the champions). 1,500 season tickets sold for 2026-27. Top flight is the stated goal.

cards.name: Coach and style of play
cards.a: A Swiss coach, 50, hired in summer 2026 after winning his home league with a newly promoted club. Switched from a defensive back five to a high-pressing back four. The fourth permanent coach since a long-serving one left in 2023. One point from four matches.
cards.b: A 55-year-old coach hired in early 2025, formerly in charge of a national team and the country's biggest club. A structured, pragmatic back three; the league's best defence last season. Talks on an extension to 2029 reported. The fourth different coach since December 2020. Four wins from four matches.

cards.name: Squad stability and icons
cards.a: Captain, 39, at the club since 2014 and captain since 2018; his contract was renewed on the club's 60th birthday. Vice-captain in his sixth season. Several regulars left in 2026, including a young striker sold for a club-record fee (about €22m). No player conduct cases found.
cards.b: Captain, 32, out since February with a torn knee ligament; a 26-year-old defender is seen as his successor. High turnover: about €108m spent on mostly young players in 2026, two long-time regulars gone. A midfielder's 2023 anti-trans social posts drew protests from fan groups, including the gay fan club.

cards.name: Academy and homegrown players
cards.a: Known for developing bought-in teenagers and selling them high. Seven academy players in the senior squad, most recruited from abroad at 16 or 17; few play first-team minutes. Past graduates include an American international. A new sporting director brought in to focus on young players.
cards.b: A modest academy: five graduates in the senior squad, four from the region; one, a Germany Under-21, plays regularly. Most players are bought cheaply or free and sold on; the president says the club must make a transfer profit every window.

cards.name: Winning and track record
cards.a: Last 10 seasons: never below 5th, runners-up five times; national cups 2017 and 2021; Champions League finals lost 2013 and 2024. Eight league titles and one European Cup (1997) in all. 1st of 18 now.
cards.b: Last 10 seasons: three in the second tier, promoted 2019; peaked at 4th and the Champions League group stage (2023-24), then 15th, 13th and 11th. No major trophy ever; one cup in the communist era (1968). 17th of 18 now.

cards.name: History and identity
cards.a: Founded 1909 by 18 young local players in a coal-and-steel working city. The first German club to win a European trophy (1966); European champions 1997; near-bankrupt in 2005, rescued. Before every match a 25,000-strong terrace sings an anthem shared with an English club.
cards.b: Founded 1966 from roots in a 1906 club; under communism the 'civilian' rival of a secret-police team. Near-bankrupt in the 1990s and 2004, when fans gave blood and donated the payments. Fans rebuilt the ground; around 28,000 sing carols there each Christmas. First top-flight season 2019.

cards.name: Following from Sacramento
cards.a: About 5,600 miles; no nonstop flights. League matches stream free in the US, mostly Saturday 6:30 am Pacific; no European matches this season. Tickets very hard: about 30,000 apply for each home match. Seven registered fan clubs abroad. Home matches move across the city 2028-29.
cards.b: About 5,500 miles; no nonstop flights. League matches stream free in the US, mostly Saturday 6:30 or 9:30 am Pacific; Champions League around weekday noon on a paid streamer. Tickets very hard: 55,000 season tickets, long waiting list. A New York fan embassy, about 40 US fan clubs.

cards.name: Where the club is heading
cards.a: 1st after four matches; the coach close to an extension to 2029. A new sporting director and a squad rebuilt around teenagers. The arms sponsorship ends in 2027. Revenue fell 12% and the club lost €22m last season; break-even forecast.
cards.b: 17th after four matches under a new coach and style. A €190m expansion of the ground, with about 18 months away from home from 2028. President in office to 2029. Self-funded and breaking even, but needing a transfer profit every window.

rules.q: One of a club's top-tier partners (pitch-side boards and stadium signage, not the shirt) is an arms maker. How much should that count against it?
o: It nearly rules the club out

rules.q: Two clubs are both controlled by their members, but one is also listed on the stock exchange. How much does that difference matter?
A club sells its best young players to richer clubs every year. How does that sit with you?
o: It counts in its favour: it develops players

rules.q: A club shares an anthem and a fan friendship with Liverpool. How much should that pull you toward it?
One club is easy to watch on US TV at good times, the other harder. How much should that count in which you follow?
Which story means more to you?
o: Rising from nothing on fans' effort
Decades of winning at the top

scen.q: It's 2031. Your club has reached the Champions League four years running, but an arms maker is still one of its top partners.
It's 2031. Your club finishes mid-table every year and hasn't won anything, but its ground is still fan-built and packed.
It's 2031. Your club was relegated last season, and every home match still sold out.
